Purpose To compare physiological responses to submaximal cycling and sprint cycling performance in women using oral contraceptives (WomenOC) and naturally cycling women (WomenNC) and to determine whether N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation mediates these responses. Methods Twenty recreationally trained women completed five exercise trials (i.e., an incremental cycling test, a familiarisation trial, a baseline performance trial and two double-blind crossover intervention trials). During the intervention trials participants supplemented with NAC or a placebo 1 h before exercise. Cardiopulmonary parameters and blood biochemistry were assessed during 40 min of fixed-intensity cycling at 105% of gas-exchange threshold and after 1-km cycling time-trial. Results WomenOC had higher ventilation ( β [95% CI] = 0.07 L·min −1 [0.01, 0.14]), malondialdehydes ( β = 12.00 mmol·L −1 [6.82, 17.17]) and C-reactive protein (1.53 mg·L −1 [0.76, 2.30]), whereas glutathione peroxidase was lower ( β = 22.62 mU·mL −1 [− 41.32, − 3.91]) compared to WomenNC during fixed-intensity cycling. Plasma thiols were higher at all timepoints after NAC ingestion compared to placebo, irrespective of group (all p < 0.001; d = 1.45 to 2.34). For WomenNC but not WomenOC, the exercise-induced increase in malondialdehyde observed in the placebo trial was blunted after NAC ingestion, with lower values at 40 min ( p = 0.018; d = 0.73). NAC did not affect cycling time-trial performance. Conclusions Blood biomarkers relating to oxidative stress and inflammation are elevated in WomenOC during exercise. There may be an increased strain on the endogenous antioxidant system during exercise, since NAC supplementation in WomenOC did not dampen the exercise-induced increase in malondialdehyde. Future investigations should explore the impact of elevated oxidative stress on exercise adaptations or recovery from exercise in WomenOC. Griffith University Open Access funding enabled and organized by CAUL and its Member Institutions issue-copyright-statement © Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2022 Introduction Prolonged high-intensity exercise is one stimulus that transiently disrupts the pro-oxidant and antioxidant (i.e., redox) environment, often resulting in oxidative stress and damage (Powers and Jackson 2008 ; Thirupathi and Pinho 2018 ). While an acute increase in exercise-induced oxidative stress may be important for training adaptations (Gomez-Cabrera et al. 2008 ), excessive production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS) during prolonged exercise has been associated with skeletal muscle fatigue (Barclay and Hansel 1991 ; Powers and Jackson 2008 ). Thus, exercise generated RONS can be described by a bell-shaped (hormesis) curve, whereby there are two endpoints of physiological function (Reid et al. 1993 ). Another factor that may moderate performance is the effect of oral contraceptives (OC) on the redox environment during exercise. Irrespective of training status, OC-use has been consistently associated with oxidative stress and damage measured at rest via blood biomarkers, e.g., elevated malondialdehyde (MDA) and low lipid-soluble antioxidants (Cauci et al. 2016 ; De Groote et al. 2009 ; Kowalska and Milnerowicz 2016 ; Palan et al. 2006 ; Quinn et al. 2018 ; Quinn et al. 2021 ). Therefore, it could be postulated that oxidative stress is exacerbated in women using OC compared to women naturally cycling during high-intensity exercise. This concurrent OC- and exercise-induced oxidative stress may drive a rightwards shift on the hormesis curve and affect skeletal muscle function and subsequent performance. However, there is paucity of experimental research in women, particularly research that controls for female sex hormones when investigating physiological responses to exercise. Although several studies have found that OC use increases oxidative stress at rest, only one study has examined the exercise-induced change in lipid peroxidation in women using OC (Massart et al. 2012 ). Massart et al. ( 2012 ) found that MDA significantly increased in both OC-users and non-users after a combat (Judo) training session, but the percent magnitude of change (i.e., pre- to post-exercise) was greater in OC non-users. However, the implications that this has on performance was not investigated (Massart et al. 2012 ), and tightly controlled research that accounts for relative work performed is required to clarify the influence of OC-use on exercise-induced oxidative stress. Characterising these physiological responses to exercise in more detail is important given that approximately 50% of female athletes use OC (Larsen et al. 2020b ). In an effort to understand the effect of RONS on skeletal muscle function, study designs have employed the use of antioxidant supplementation (Matuszczak et al. 2005 ; Paschalis et al. 2018 ). Associated findings suggest that when the concentration of exercise-generated RONS is high, the administered antioxidant may protect muscle cells against RONS-related fatiging mechanisms (e.g., calcium sensitivity) and thus enhance performance (Andrade et al. 2001 ; Matuszczak et al. 2005 ). One such antioxidant is N-acetylcysteine (NAC), which has been shown to protect cells against oxidative insults by acting as a cysteine donor for the (re)synthesis of glutathione, mitochondrial sulfane sulphur production and/or to a lesser extent, a direct scavenging ability (Aldini et al. 2018 ). In exercise physiology research conducted predominately in men, NAC has been established as an ergogenic aid in hand-grip exercise (Matuszczak et al. 2005 ), intermittent high-intensity running (Cobley et al. 2011 ; Rhodes et al. 2019 ) and high-intensity cycling exercise (McKenna et al. 2006 ; Medved et al. 2004b ; Paschalis et al. 2018 ; Slattery et al. 2014 ). More recently, the use of NAC as an ergogenic aid has been demonstrated to be more effective in male participants with a glutathione deficiency compared to those with normal or high glutathione levels (Margaritelis et al. 2020 ; Paschalis et al. 2018 ). As such, the available research suggests that NAC supplementation may have a positive impact on exercise performance for women using OC given there is preliminary evidence demonstrating low glutathione and glutathione peroxidase (GPx) in OC-users at rest (Kowalska and Milnerowicz 2016 ; Quinn et al. 2021 ). Our primary aim was to determine whether there are differences in blood biomarkers of oxidant damage and antioxidants during heavy, fixed-intensity exercise in women naturally cycling compared to women using OC. We were also interested in exploring whether acute (i.e., 1 h prior to exercise) NAC supplementation alters blood biomarkers during fixed-intensity cycling in the two groups, and whether there was any subsequent effect on 1-km cycling time trial (TT) performance. It was hypothesized that oxidant damage would change similarly for both groups in response to exercise; however, women using OC would have higher absolute oxidant damage measured in the blood after exercise compared to naturally cycling women. It was also hypothesized that NAC supplementation would dampen the increase in biomarkers of oxidant damage in both groups, however, improve cycling TT performance only in women using OC.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Oral contraceptive (OC) use and exercise-induced oxidative stress in women
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Oral contraceptive (OC) use is consistently associated with oxidative stress and damage, both at rest and exacerbated during high-intensity exercise in women, characterized by elevated malondialdehyde (MDA) and C-reactive protein (CRP), and lower glutathione peroxidase (GPx). This is primarily attributed to the metabolism of exogenous sex hormones (ethinyl-estradiol and progestin) in the liver, which can overwhelm conjugant pathways, leading to increased liver proteins, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS), and oxidant damage. This suggests an increased strain on the endogenous antioxidant system in WomenOC. The lower GPx observed in WomenOC is linked to the use of exogenous sex steroids and/or suppression of endogenous sex steroids. An increased ventilatory drive in WomenOC during exercise is suggested to result from the stimulatory effect of synthetic progestin on respiratory mechanisms. N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation protects cells against oxidative insults by acting as a cysteine donor for glutathione resynthesis and mitochondrial sulfane sulfur production. NAC effectively blunts exercise-induced MDA increase in naturally cycling women (WomenNC), but not in WomenOC, which may reflect an OC-induced depletion of the body's endogenous antioxidant capacity due to compounded RONS production. NAC may also preserve cycling efficiency by maintaining ion transporter activity, reducing oxidant interference, and/or improving calcium release within contracting myofibers.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study involved fixed-intensity cycling at 105% of gas-exchange threshold and acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation. Women using oral contraceptives (WomenOC) were tested on days 13–18 of active pill-taking to minimize transient biomarker shifts. Naturally cycling women (WomenNC) were tested in the mid-luteal phase, verified by progesterone levels. NAC was acutely administered as two oral doses (70 mg·kg −1 and 35 mg·kg −1 body mass) 1 hour prior to exercise, a regimen previously shown to elevate cysteine-related thiols. The absolute increase in malondialdehyde (MDA) during exercise in the placebo trial was larger in WomenOC (+5.22 mmol·L −1, 31% relative increase) compared to WomenNC (+2.86 mmol·L −1, 51% relative increase). Ventilation during fixed-intensity cycling was 2.8 L·min −1 higher in WomenOC at Ex 40, with the magnitude of difference dependent on exercise duration. It was suggested that a higher NAC dose might be required for WomenOC to achieve similar effects as in WomenNC, though this carries a higher risk of gastrointestinal discomfort.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The exercise-induced increase in malondialdehyde (MDA) was specifically blunted after N-acetylcysteine (NAC) ingestion in naturally cycling women (WomenNC), but not in women using oral contraceptives (WomenOC). WomenNC were tested in the mid-luteal phase, while WomenOC were tested on days 13–18 of active pill-taking, due to known differences in oxidative stress across OC use weeks. Oral contraceptive (OC) use was consistently associated with lower glutathione peroxidase (GPx) and higher C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, irrespective of NAC supplementation or exercise timepoint. Vascular oxidative stress, related to superoxide and nitric oxide production or subsequent protein modification (e.g., 3-nitrotyrosine), was not significantly affected by OC use. The differential effect of NAC on MDA highlights that the impact of OC use on biological function and redox pathways is specific, and NAC's efficacy can depend on baseline glutathione concentrations, sex-specific redox processes, exercise task, supplementation duration, and training status.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Recreationally trained and active women aged 18–35 years, including those with natural menstrual cycles (WomenNC, n=11) and those using combined, monophasic oral contraceptives for at least 12 months (WomenOC, n=9). This population is relevant given approximately 50% of female athletes use oral contraceptives. Exclusions included individuals at high risk for vigorous exercise, using antioxidant/vitamin supplements, smoking, using non-monophasic combined OC, or having a history of endocrinological, musculoskeletal, inflammatory, respiratory, or cardiovascular disorders.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Oral contraceptive (OC) use is associated with elevated blood biomarkers of oxidative stress and inflammation (e.g., C-reactive protein) at rest and during exercise, alongside elevated ventilation during fixed-intensity cycling. This suggests an increased strain on the endogenous antioxidant system and a potential shift towards a new physiological redox set point in women using OC (WomenOC). While acute exercise-induced oxidative stress can be beneficial for training adaptations, excessive production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS) during prolonged exercise can lead to skeletal muscle fatigue. The concurrent OC- and exercise-induced oxidative stress in WomenOC may negatively affect skeletal muscle function and performance, although no deleterious effect on sprint cycling performance was observed in this specific study. Chronically elevated oxidative stress is likely harmful for biological systems, and the long-term implications of altered redox homeostasis in WomenOC, particularly concerning health, exercise adaptations, and recovery, require further investigation. The study aims to provide foundational understanding of these female-specific physiological differences.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: The findings indicate an adverse risk for women using oral contraceptives due to consistently elevated oxidative stress and inflammation, alongside an increased strain on their endogenous antioxidant system during exercise. Biomarkers such as malondialdehyde (MDA) and C-reactive protein (CRP) demonstrate diagnostic utility in identifying this altered redox state.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: Oral contraceptive (OC) use has been consistently associated with oxidative stress and damage measured at rest via blood biomarkers (e.g., elevated malondialdehyde and low lipid-soluble antioxidants). The study demonstrated good reliability for 1-km time trial performance (ICC = 0.90, SEM = 1.7 s) and reported low intra-assay coefficients of variation for various biochemical assays, including serum oestradiol and progesterone (4.04%), plasma glutathione peroxidase (2.6%), free thiols (6.4%), malondialdehyde (8.0%), 3-nitrotyrosine (4.8%), and total glutathione (4.6%). The homogeneity of the study groups (e.g., aerobic fitness) enhances confidence in the finding of lower glutathione peroxidase in WomenOC being related to OC use. The crossover experimental design helped account for individual variation. However, limitations include the potential for the malondialdehyde assay to react with other plasma aldehydes, the total antioxidant capacity assay not identifying specific antioxidants, and the selection of blood biomarkers and sampling timepoints (e.g., lack of multiple post-exercise samples). High attrition rates affected participant numbers. Future tightly controlled research that accounts for relative work performed is required to further clarify the influence of OC-use on exercise-induced oxidative stress, and to explore the impact of elevated oxidative stress on exercise adaptations or recovery in WomenOC.
recommended_alternatives: Other key redox biomarkers including reduced and oxidized glutathione (for interpreting total glutathione changes)
Measurements of pH and bicarbonate (to interrogate potential implications to acid–base balance in OC users)
Assays that identify specific antioxidants (instead of Total Antioxidant Capacity)
Alternative malondialdehyde assays that specifically measure lipid peroxides
